plain: Colorado now checks mail ballots by comparing the signature on the return envelope to the one on file. Amendment 84 would also require an ID number on the envelope.

short_version.text: Colorado checks mail ballots by signature today and did not count 1.4 percent of returned mail ballots in 2024. Amendment 84 adds an ID number. In Texas, a similar rule sent rejections up sharply at first, and they fell after envelopes improved. No one has estimated the effect in Colorado.

agree_means: Every mail voter would write the last four digits of a Social Security number, or a Colorado driver's license or ID number, on the envelope. A ballot with a missing or unmatched number would not count until the voter fixed it.
disagree_means: Signature checks stay as the only test for mail ballots, with the current letter-and-fix process for problems.

example.text: You would write a number on your return envelope: the last four digits of your Social Security number, or your Colorado driver's license or ID card number. If it's missing or wrong, the county contacts you, and you have until eight days after Election Day to fix it.

stakes.text: Texas added an ID-number rule in 2021. In its March 2022 primary, 12.4% of returned mail ballots were rejected, versus 0.8% in 2020. A Brennan Center study, which Votebeat calls nonpartisan, found about 90% of voters whose mail ballot or application was rejected did not vote another way.

stakes.text: Georgia replaced signature matching with ID numbers. State data put its May 2022 primary rejections at 2.6%, up from just over 1% in 2020. An early Post count found 1%, down from 4.3% in 2018. In 2024 the rate was 1.7%.

sources.title: Gauging the Effects of SB 202 on Voting in Georgia (Hood and McKee, MIT Election Data and Science Lab)
sources.quote: SB 202 altered verification for absentee applications and ballots from signature verification to use of a driver’s license or state ID number.

sources.title: May primary was the biggest test yet for Georgia's new voting law (WABE)
sources.quote: More than 2.6 percent of absentee ballots were rejected in May, according to election data from the Georgia Secretary of State. That’s up from just over 1 percent in the June 2020 primary.

sources.title: Rejection Rates for Absentee Ballots in GA Far Lower than in 2018 Primary Elections (Election Law Blog)
sources.quote: An analysis by The Post shows the rates went from roughly 4.3 percent to 1 percent.

stakes.text: In 2024 a Mesa County mail carrier and a friend were accused of forging stolen ballots. Signature checks caught 12 of 16; three were counted. The case shows both that forged ballots can get through and that signature checks can catch them.

sources.title: Two Mesa County women arrested in alleged fraudulent mail-in ballot scheme (Colorado Politics)
sources.quote: Twelve 12 were caught in the signature verification process, but three have been counted and cannot be reversed

case_for.text: Supporters say ID numbers are steadier than a judge's opinion of handwriting, and that most voters already have a card or know their number.

unknowns.text: No one has estimated how many Colorado ballots the rule would reject. Texas limits mail voting to certain voters, so its results may not carry over to Colorado, where every active voter gets a ballot.

research_notes: Colorado-specific reasons for 2024 rejections were not found; the EAC national table (40.7% signature, 17.8% late) was not used because it is not Colorado data. The 2020 uncured-signature count (21,838) is the latest Colorado split I could fetch. EAC figures for Colorado, Texas and Georgia come from table rows in the EAVS PDF (verify against the PDF's own text layer). Georgia's May 2022 rate is 2.6% in WABE (Secretary of State data) but a Washington Post analysis quoted by the Election Law Blog (read in browser, not used in text) found about 1% as of two days after the primary, so Georgia figures depend on timing. Colorado Newsline, WABE and the Election Law Blog returned 403 to scripted fetches. Claude in Chrome was not connected, so I read them in the built-in browser pane, in my own tab (marked via browser). The AJC Georgia article was scrambled by its paywall and was dropped. Review: the Brennan Center description uses Votebeat's word 'nonpartisan'. The Mesa County case figures come from arrest affidavits as reported; the source's '12 + 3' does not add to its stated 16 ballots, which I left as reported.
